::: {.lead}
Today the lab computers are Rami's desk. Each student gets the same build,
`PocketQuest_1.3.apk`, and the same test plan with eight test cases. One of
the test cases hides a real bug. In lecture 25 you planned a test
environment with emulators and real devices. In this seminar you **do** it:
you create an Android Virtual Device, start it, install the build, run the
test cases, collect the evidence and write a bug report. You work alone.
Each section is one step of the seminar and ends with a task; at the end
you hand in a short test report.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary android-studio avd system-image emulator adb apk logcat game-build >}}

## 26.1 Create and start the virtual device

Steps 1–3 happen in Android Studio (@fig-steps).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 26.1 — Steps 1–3"}
1. Open Android Studio → **Device Manager** → **Create device**.
2. Choose the device profile and the **system image** (download it once),
   name the AVD, for example `P5_API_30`.
3. Press **Start**. The first start (a **cold boot**) takes longer; later
   starts use a saved state (**quick boot**).

From a terminal, the same AVD starts with `emulator -avd P5_API_30`;
`emulator -list-avds` lists the names.
:::

![The steps of the seminar.](images/seminar-steps.png){#fig-steps width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 26.1 — The first boot in the lab"}
1. Rami creates `P5_API_30`: 720 × 1600, 4 GB, Android 11.
2. The system image is about 1 GB: on the lab network the download takes
   two minutes, so the teacher downloads it before the seminar.
3. The first boot takes 18 seconds; the home screen of Android 11 appears.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"The emulator does not start." Often virtualization is off in the BIOS, or
the computer has too little free RAM. Close other programs, and ask the lab
technician about virtualization.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Steps 1–3"}
On the lab computer (or in **Emulator Lab**), create and start
`P5_API_30`. Write how long the first boot took.

*Your result:* a running emulator and one time.
:::

## 26.2 Install the build

Step 4 puts the build on the emulator (@fig-adb).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 26.2 — Installing an APK"}
Two ways:

- **Drag and drop** the `.apk` file onto the emulator window.
- **adb:** `adb devices` must list the emulator (for example
  `emulator-5554 device`); then `adb install PocketQuest_1.3.apk`.
  `adb uninstall` with the package name removes the app again.
:::

![Commands of the seminar.](images/adb-commands.png){#fig-adb width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 26.2 — No devices"}
1. A student types `adb install PocketQuest_1.3.apk` and sees
   `adb: no devices/emulators found`.
2. `adb devices` shows an empty list: the emulator was closed.
3. After `emulator -avd P5_API_30` and a new `adb devices`, the install
   prints `Success`, and the Pocket Quest icon appears.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/adb-lab.html" poster="sims/adb-lab.png" title="Emulator Lab: run Pocket Quest 1.3" height="720" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Installing from the wrong folder: `failed to stat … No such file`. Run adb
in the folder of the APK, or write the full path.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Step 4"}
Install the build twice: once by drag and drop, once with `adb install`
(uninstall it in between). Copy the output of `adb devices`.

*Your result:* two installs and one line of output.
:::

## 26.3 Run the test cases and collect evidence

Steps 5 and 6: test, and keep the proof.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 26.3 — Testing on the emulator"}
- Follow the test plan **in order**, and mark each case pass or fail.
- The emulator's **extended controls** change the device: rotation, the
  battery level, the location, the network speed and delay, a phone call.
- Collect **evidence**: a **screenshot** of the problem, and the lines of
  **Logcat** (`adb logcat`, or the Logcat window of Android Studio) from
  the moment it happened.
- Repeat a failed case once, to be sure the steps make it happen again.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 26.3 — Test case 7"}
1. Test case 7: "Start a race, then turn the device to landscape."
2. The race freezes; after five seconds Android says *Pocket Quest isn't
   responding*.
3. Logcat shows `E/Unity: NullReferenceException: RaceHud.OnScreenRotate
   () (at RaceHud.cs:118)`.
4. Rami repeats the steps: the freeze happens again. Rami saves a
   screenshot and the 20 lines of the log around the error.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Copying the whole log, thousands of lines. Copy the lines around the error,
with the time, so that the developer finds it at once.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Steps 5–6"}
1. In **Emulator Lab**, run test case 7, then read the log and take a
   screenshot.
2. On the lab emulator, change the network to a slow, delayed connection
   in the extended controls, and race once. What changes?

*Your result:* a screenshot, the error line and one observation.
:::

## 26.4 Write the bug report

Step 7: a developer must be able to repeat the bug from the report alone
(@fig-report).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 26.4 — A good bug report"}
- **Title:** what goes wrong, in one line.
- **Build:** the version and the build number.
- **Device:** the device or AVD and the OS version.
- **Steps:** numbered, from the start.
- **Expected** and **actual** result.
- **Attached:** a screenshot and the lines of the log.

One bug per report.
:::

![A good bug report.](images/bug-report.png){#fig-report width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 26.4 — From \"it broke\" to a report"}
1. First draft: "The game broke when I turned it."
2. Rami adds the build (42), the AVD (`P5_API_30`, Android 11), the two
   steps, expected (the race goes on) and actual (freeze), and attaches the
   screenshot and the log.
3. The developer repeats it in two minutes and fixes `RaceHud.cs` line 118.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing your opinion instead of the facts ("the HUD code is bad"). Report
what you did and what you saw; the developer finds the cause.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your test report"}
Write a one-page test report: the test environment (build, AVD, OS), the
eight test cases with pass or fail, and one complete bug report.

*Your result:* a one-page test report.
:::

## Case study: Report Doctor

After the emulator session, six bug reports reach Byte Bay's developers: one
without the device, one without steps, one that says only "looks bad", one
without a build number, one with three bugs at once, and one without any
log or screenshot. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
reports. In the mini-game below you decide what must be fixed in each one.

## Further reading

Android Developers, "Android Debug Bridge (adb)" and "Run apps on the
Android Emulator" (developer.android.com). Kaner, Falk and Nguyen, *Testing
Computer Software* (2nd ed., 1999), the chapter on reporting and analysing
bugs.

## Exercises

1. Where do you create an AVD in Android Studio?
2. What is the difference between a cold boot and a quick boot?
3. Name two ways to install an APK on the emulator.
4. What must `adb devices` show before `adb install` works?
5. What does `adb: no devices/emulators found` mean?
6. Name three things the extended controls can change.
7. Why do you repeat a failed test case?
8. Which part of the log do you copy into a report?
9. List the parts of a good bug report.
10. Why only one bug per report?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. In the Device Manager.
2. A cold boot starts Android from the beginning; a quick boot loads a saved
   state and is faster.
3. Drag and drop the file onto the emulator; `adb install`.
4. The emulator with the state `device`.
5. No emulator or phone is connected (for example the emulator is closed).
6. For example rotation, battery, location, network speed and delay.
7. To be sure the steps make the bug happen again.
8. The lines around the error, with the time.
9. Title, build, device and OS, steps, expected, actual, attachments.
10. So that each bug can be fixed, tested and closed alone.
:::
